audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Officer Lin from the Campus Security Office, and I'd like to spend a few minutes on something that affects almost every student at some point: losing things. Last semester, our office received more than eight hundred items, but fewer than half were ever claimed. The most common items were umbrellas, water bottles, and earphones, but we also received forty-two student ID cards.

So here's what we recommend. First, put your name or email on anything valuable. A simple sticker makes it much easier for us to contact you. Second, if you lose something, check our online lost and found page before you visit us. We upload photos of new items every weekday by noon. Third, if you lose your student ID, report it on the student portal right away, so no one else can use it to borrow books or enter your dorm. Finally, please remember that we keep items for only sixty days. After that, they're donated or recycled.

passage: For years, students at Ming Feng University who lost an umbrella or a calculator had only one option: walk to the security office, describe the item to a staff member, and hope it was sitting on a shelf in the back room. This semester, that process has changed. In September, the Student Affairs Office launched FindIt, an online lost and found system that lets students search for items by location, date, and category.

Under the new system, any staff member who receives a lost item takes a photo of it and uploads it within twenty-four hours. Valuable items, such as phones and wallets, are shown only as general descriptions to prevent false claims. Students who believe an item is theirs must answer a few questions, such as the color of the phone case or the contents of the wallet, before they can collect it.

The results have been encouraging. According to the Student Affairs Office, the return rate rose from 38 percent last spring to 61 percent in the first two months of this semester. "Before, many students simply gave up because they didn't know where to look," said Hsu Mei-ling, the system's project manager. "Now they can check from their phones in a minute."

Not everyone is satisfied, however. Some students say the photos are sometimes blurry, and items found in department buildings still take several days to appear online. The office plans to train department assistants to upload items directly by next semester. It is also considering a feature that would send automatic alerts when an item matching a student's description is uploaded.
